lessons.title: What Is Programming?
lessons.introduction: Programming is the craft of writing clear, unambiguous step-by-step instructions that tell a computer or microcontroller exactly how to solve a problem.
objectives: Explain what programming means in plain engineering terms.
Distinguish human natural language from precise machine instructions.
Identify how a program turns sensor inputs into physical actions on an Arduino.
conceptExplanation: Computers and microcontrollers cannot guess your intentions. Even a tiny chip like the ATmega328P inside an Arduino Uno R3 can execute millions of operations per second, yet it has zero common sense on its own.

Programming bridges human goals and electronic hardware. Instead of saying 'turn on the fan when it feels hot', a programmer writes exact rules: read the temperature sensor, compare the value against 30 degrees Celsius, and set the motor control pin HIGH.
lessons.analogy: Think of programming like writing a recipe for a kitchen robot that takes every word literally. If you forget to say 'remove the egg shell', it will drop the whole egg into the bowl.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Every Arduino program is written as a sequence of exact statements grouped inside functions.
rules: Every instruction must follow exact spelling and capitalization.
Most individual instructions end with a semicolon (;).
Curly braces { } group related instructions together.

codeExamples.title: Turning On the Built-in LED
codeExamples.description: This minimal Arduino sketch tells the microcontroller to prepare pin 13 and send voltage to light its onboard LED.

lineByLine.explanation: Starts the one-time startup block that runs when the board powers on.
Tells the microcontroller that digital pin 13 will send electrical signals out.
Sets pin 13 to HIGH voltage (5V on Uno R3), turning the onboard LED on.
Required repeating block; currently empty because the LED stays on.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Every automated device — from a smart greenhouse watering pump to a line-following robot — relies on small, exact programmed instructions executing continuously.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the board understands vague intent
commonMistakes.fix: Break every goal into explicit, testable steps with exact pin numbers and thresholds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement
commonMistakes.fix: Check the end of each line inside { } for a missing ';'.

tryItYourself.title: m01_first_instruction.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change HIGH to LOW inside setup() to see how a single word changes the hardware instruction.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: With HIGH, the onboard LED on pin 13 turns on and stays lit after uploading in Arduino IDE. With LOW, the LED remains off.

exercises.prompt: Why must programming instructions be written with strict precision?
options: Microcontrollers execute instructions literally and cannot guess human intent.
Arduino boards only accept instructions written in all capital letters.
Shorter programs automatically use less electricity.
Computers randomly skip unclear instructions.
exercises.explanation: Hardware processors follow instructions literally; ambiguous or malformed instructions either fail to compile or produce unintended behavior.

exercises.prompt: Complete the statement that turns digital pin 13 ON.
exercises.explanation: HIGH sets a digital output pin to its active voltage (5V on Uno R3, 3.3V on ESP32).

summary: Programming means writing exact, step-by-step instructions for a computer or microcontroller.
Microcontrollers execute commands fast and reliably, but literally.
In Arduino C++, setup() configures hardware once and loop() runs continuously.

lessons.title: What Is a Program?
lessons.introduction: A program is a complete, organized collection of instructions and data stored together to accomplish a defined task.
objectives: Define the parts of a program: data, instructions, and control flow.
Recognize why Arduino programs are called 'sketches' saved with the .ino extension.
Trace a simple two-step blinking program from top to bottom.
conceptExplanation: A single instruction like digitalWrite(13, HIGH); only does one tiny action. A program combines many instructions, named values (data), and timing or decision rules into a working system.

In the Arduino ecosystem, a program is called a sketch and saved in a folder with a .ino file. Behind the scenes, Arduino IDE compiles your sketch into binary machine code and flashes it into the board's flash memory.
lessons.analogy: If a single line of code is one musical note, a program is the complete sheet music that tells the orchestra what to play and when to pause.

syntaxExplanation.summary: An Arduino program combines declarations at the top with setup() and loop().
rules: Data declarations (like pin numbers) sit cleanly near the top of the program.
setup() prepares pins and communication once.
loop() repeats the main behavior indefinitely while powered.

codeExamples.title: Complete Blink Program
codeExamples.description: A full Arduino program that alternates pin 13 between HIGH and LOW every half second.

lineByLine.explanation: Stores the pin number 13 under a readable name so the program is easy to update.
Configures pin 13 for output inside setup().
Pauses program execution for 500 milliseconds (0.5 seconds).
Turns the LED off before waiting another 500 ms and repeating.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Status beacons on autonomous rovers use simple repeating programs to indicate battery health or active telemetry.

commonMistakes.fix: Without the pause after LOW, loop() immediately jumps back to HIGH in microseconds, so the LED appears constantly on.
setup() runs only once on reset; repeating tasks belong in loop().

tryItYourself.title: m01_blink_program.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change both delay values from 500 to 250 to double the blinking speed.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: The LED blinks on for 0.25 s and off for 0.25 s (2 blinks per second) after uploading via Arduino IDE.

exercises.prompt: What happens if you delete the second delay(500); at the bottom of loop()?
options: The LED turns off for only a few microseconds and looks permanently ON to human eyes.
The LED blinks twice as slowly.
The Arduino refuses to compile the program.
The LED stays permanently OFF.
exercises.explanation: Right after setting pin 13 LOW, loop() restarts immediately and sets it HIGH again in microseconds.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the lines to form a clean blinking cycle inside loop().
exercises.explanation: You must turn the LED ON, pause so it is visible, turn it OFF, and pause again before repeating.

summary: A program combines named data with ordered instructions to achieve a goal.
Arduino programs are saved as .ino sketches and compiled into machine code.
Every transition in a repeating cycle needs appropriate timing.

diagram.caption: How an Arduino microcontroller runs setup() once and repeats loop() continuously.

lessons.title: How Computers Execute Instructions
lessons.introduction: Understanding sequential execution and the fetch-decode-execute cycle helps you predict exactly what your microcontroller will do at every millisecond.
objectives: Trace top-to-bottom sequential execution inside a function.
Explain the role of the CPU clock, Flash memory, and SRAM on an Arduino.
Predict how changing instruction order changes program output.
conceptExplanation: A microcontroller reads instructions from Flash memory one by one in order, decodes each instruction, and executes it using its CPU and temporary SRAM memory. Unless a branch (if), loop, or function call redirects it, execution always moves strictly top to bottom.
On an Arduino Uno R3 running at 16 MHz, the processor performs up to 16 million clock cycles per second. That speed is why a tiny missing delay or wrong line order happens faster than you can blink.
lessons.analogy: Execution is like a finger sliding down a checklist one line at a time — it never skips ahead unless a rule explicitly tells it to jump.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Statements inside a block run in exact top-to-bottom order.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
int count = 1;       // 1st
count = count + 2;   // 2nd -> count is now 3
Serial.println(count); // 3rd -> prints 3
rules: Order matters: printing a variable before updating it shows the old value.
Flash memory stores your compiled program even when power is removed.
SRAM holds temporary variables and resets every time the board loses power.

codeExamples.title: Tracing Sequential Execution with Serial
codeExamples.description: Prints numbered steps to the Arduino Serial Monitor to prove top-to-bottom execution.

lineByLine.explanation: Opens USB serial communication at 9600 bits per second.
Creates an integer variable in SRAM initialized to 0.
Prints 0 first because steps has not been increased yet.
Adds 5 to steps and stores 5 back into SRAM before the second print.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Robotics startup sequences depend on strict order: you must initialize the IMU sensor and calibrate zero-drift before enabling drive motors.

commonMistakes.mistake: Printing a result before computing it
commonMistakes.fix: Ensure calculations run before Serial.println() or digitalWrite().
Code lives in Flash (non-volatile); live sensor variables live in SRAM (cleared on reset).

tryItYourself.title: m01_execution_order.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add one more line that adds 10 to steps and prints the new value.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Serial Monitor displays 0, then 5, then 15 on separate lines once uploaded and opened at 9600 baud.

exercises.prompt: What two numbers are printed to Serial Monitor?
options: 7 and 14
4 and 8
4 and 7
7 and 9
exercises.explanation: x starts at 4, becomes 7 before the first print, then doubles to 14 before the second print.

exercises.prompt: Where does an Arduino store your compiled program so it survives when unplugged?
options: Flash memory
SRAM
USB cable
Serial Monitor
exercises.explanation: Compiled machine instructions are written to non-volatile Flash memory; variables live in volatile SRAM.

summary: Microcontrollers execute instructions sequentially from top to bottom.
Changing the order of statements changes the resulting state and output.
Program code persists in Flash memory while variables reset in SRAM on power loss.

lessons.title: What Is C++?
lessons.introduction: Arduino sketches are written in C++, one of the world's most widely used systems and robotics languages.
objectives: Explain why C++ is used for microcontrollers and robotics.
Recognize that Arduino adds helpful hardware functions on top of standard C++.
Identify basic C++ building blocks inside an Arduino sketch.
conceptExplanation: C++ is a compiled, high-performance programming language that gives engineers direct control over memory and hardware timing while still supporting clean abstractions like functions and classes.

Many beginners think 'Arduino' is a completely separate language. In reality, Arduino sketches are standard C++ compiled with GCC/Clang, plus a convenient core library that provides pinMode(), digitalWrite(), millis(), and Serial.
lessons.analogy: C++ is the engine under the hood; the Arduino core library is the steering wheel and dashboard that makes driving hardware approachable.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Standard C++ data types, math, and control structures work natively inside Arduino sketches.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
int speed = 120;           // Standard C++ variable
if (speed > 100) {         // Standard C++ decision
  analogWrite(9, speed);   // Arduino hardware function
}
rules: C++ is case-sensitive: speed and Speed are two different identifiers.
C++ is statically typed: every variable must declare its data type (e.g., int, float, bool).
Code is compiled before running, catching syntax errors early.

codeExamples.title: Standard C++ Inside an Arduino Sketch
codeExamples.description: Combines standard C++ arithmetic and a conditional check with Arduino Serial output.

lineByLine.explanation: Standard C++ integer variable declaration.
Standard C++ conditional expression evaluating true or false.
Arduino Serial object method that sends text over USB.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Learning C++ through Arduino transfers directly to ROS2 robotics, embedded firmware, game engines, and aerospace control software.

commonMistakes.fix: Always match exact casing: pinMode works, PinMode fails to compile.
Unlike Python or JavaScript, C++ requires a type such as int or float when creating a variable.

tryItYourself.title: m01_cpp_basics.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change voltageMv to 4100 and add an else block that prints "Low battery".
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: When voltageMv is 4100 and an else branch is added, Serial Monitor prints 'Low battery'.

exercises.prompt: What is the relationship between C++ and Arduino programming?
options: Arduino sketches are written in C++ using an added library of hardware functions.
Arduino replaces C++ with JavaScript.
C++ only runs on desktop computers, never on microcontrollers.
Arduino code is interpreted line-by-line without compiling.
exercises.explanation: Arduino uses a real C++ compiler along with a hardware abstraction library (pinMode, digitalWrite, Serial, etc.).

exercises.prompt: Find the C++ error in this snippet.
options: sensorValue is missing its C++ data type (e.g., int sensorValue = 512;).
Serial.begin(9600) must always be on line 1.
512 is too large for an Arduino.
void setup() should be named void start().
exercises.explanation: C++ is statically typed, so every new variable must declare its type before or when assigned.

summary: Arduino programming is built directly on standard compiled C++.
C++ requires explicit data types and exact capitalization.
Mastering C++ fundamentals first makes every Arduino library easier to understand.

lessons.title: Introduction to Arduino Programming
lessons.introduction: Arduino boards connect software logic directly to real-world voltages, sensors, lights, and motors through physical I/O pins.
objectives: Identify digital pins, analog pins, power pins, and GND on an Arduino board.
Explain why every circuit needs a shared Ground (GND) reference.
Understand the difference between reading an input and driving an output.
conceptExplanation: Unlike a laptop that interacts mainly with a screen and keyboard, an Arduino interacts with the physical world through General-Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) pins.

Digital pins read or write two binary states: LOW (0V) or HIGH (typically 5V on Uno/Mega or 3.3V on ESP32). Analog input pins measure continuous voltages across a range of numbers so you can read light levels, temperature, or knob positions.
lessons.analogy: Think of GND as sea level: voltage is like altitude. Without a common sea level (shared GND), two devices cannot agree on how high a signal is.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Arduino hardware control follows two steps: configure pin direction, then read or write.
syntaxExplanation.pattern:
pinMode(pinNumber, MODE);          // INPUT, OUTPUT, or INPUT_PULLUP
digitalWrite(pinNumber, HIGH);     // Send voltage out
int state = digitalRead(pinNumber);// Read voltage in
rules: Always connect GND between your Arduino and external sensors or power supplies.
Use a 220–330 ohm resistor in series with LEDs to protect both the LED and the pin.
Never power heavy DC motors directly from a GPIO pin.

codeExamples.title: Input and Output Together
codeExamples.description: Configures pin 2 as a button input and pin 13 as an LED output.

lineByLine.explanation: Activates an internal resistor so pin 2 reads HIGH when idle and LOW when pressed to GND.
Allows pin 13 to drive an LED.
Checks whether the button is currently connecting pin 2 to GND.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Limit switches on 3D printers and robotic arms use this exact INPUT_PULLUP pattern to detect when an axis reaches its home position safely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to connect a common GND
commonMistakes.fix: Always tie GND rails together across breadboard, sensors, and board.

commonMistakes.mistake: Connecting an LED without a resistor
commonMistakes.fix: Always add a 220–330 ohm resistor in series with standard 5mm LEDs.

tryItYourself.title: m01_arduino_intro.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Invert the logic so the LED stays ON when the button is NOT pressed and turns OFF when pressed.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: When inverted, the LED stays lit by default and turns off whenever the button connected to pin 2 and GND is held down.

exercises.prompt: Why do we put a 220-ohm resistor in series with an LED on an Arduino output pin?
options: To limit electrical current so neither the LED nor the microcontroller pin burns out.
To make the LED blink automatically.
To convert analog signals into digital signals.
To increase the voltage from 5V to 12V.
exercises.explanation: An LED has very low resistance once lit; without a current-limiting resistor, excess current can damage both the LED and GPIO pin.

exercises.prompt: Select the line that configures pin 7 as a digital output.
options: pinMode(7, OUTPUT);
digitalWrite(7, OUTPUT);
pinMode(OUTPUT, 7);
setPin(7, OUT);
exercises.explanation: pinMode takes the pin number first and the mode (INPUT, OUTPUT, or INPUT_PULLUP) second.

summary: Arduino GPIO pins bridge software logic to physical circuits.
Digital pins handle HIGH/LOW binary signals; analog pins measure continuous voltage ranges.
Always protect LEDs with resistors and share a common GND.

lessons.title: Understanding Source Code
lessons.introduction: Source code is the human-readable text you write, whereas machine code is the binary instructions the microcontroller actually executes.
objectives: Differentiate human-readable source code from compiled machine code.
Read indentation, comments, identifiers, and braces to understand unfamiliar sketches.
Recognize how the compiler checks your source code before upload.
conceptExplanation: You write source code in plain text using English-like keywords such as if, while, int, and return. Microcontrollers cannot directly read English words; they execute binary patterns (0s and 1s).

When you click Verify in Arduino IDE, a C++ compiler translates your source code into machine code (.hex or .bin). If you make a syntax mistake — like a missing brace or typo — the compiler stops and reports the exact line number so you can fix it.
lessons.analogy: Source code is like an architect's blueprint that humans can read and edit; the compiler is the factory that turns that blueprint into the finished physical chip instructions.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Clean source code uses meaningful names, consistent indentation, and brief comments.
rules: Indentation does not change how C++ runs, but it makes nesting immediately clear to humans.
Comments (// ...) are ignored by the compiler and use zero memory on the Arduino.
Compiler error messages point near the first syntax mistake — always read the first error first.

codeExamples.title: Clean, Well-Documented Source Code
codeExamples.description: Demonstrates readable naming, indentation, and concise comments.

lineByLine.explanation: Single-line comment explaining intent; stripped out during compilation.
Replaces a 'magic number' with a descriptive constant.
Visually separates lines belonging inside setup() and loop().

lessons.realWorldApplication: In real engineering teams, source code is read ten times more often than it is written — readable code makes debugging hardware faults dramatically faster.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using cryptic names like a, b, x1
commonMistakes.fix: Use descriptive names like MOTOR_LEFT_PIN or distanceCm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring compiler errors after the first one
commonMistakes.fix: Fix the very first error reported; later errors are often cascade effects.

tryItYourself.title: m01_source_code.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Rename BLINK_MS to HEARTBEAT_MS everywhere in the sketch and set it to 300.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: After renaming consistently and uploading in Arduino IDE, the LED blinks every 300 ms with cleaner self-documenting code.

exercises.prompt: Do comments (// ...) take up Flash memory or slow down your Arduino?
options: No — the compiler strips comments completely before generating machine code.
Yes — every comment slows down loop() by 1 millisecond.
Yes — comments fill up SRAM.
Comments are only allowed in setup().
exercises.explanation: Comments exist solely for human readers and are completely discarded by the C++ compiler.

exercises.prompt: Write a single C++ constant declaration named SENSOR_PIN with the integer value 4.
exercises.explanation: const int SENSOR_PIN = 4; declares an unchangeable integer constant with a clear name.

summary: Source code is human-readable text; the compiler translates it into binary machine code.
Comments and indentation cost zero microcontroller memory.
Always read and fix the first compiler error message first.
